name: Omar Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a usual factory shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, 58, and I tend a candle-filling machine that pours hot wax into glass jars. I finished secondary school and came onto the machine from packing this year, so the lead still checks my first wick setting. I like the quiet row of even flames in the test room, but clearing a wax spill beside the hot pump is miserable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do work and money sit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Marta cleans classrooms, and our children are grown with homes of their own. The candle job pays around the ordinary operator rate, we have about three months of expenses saved and there are some other factories nearby. I have never used AI tools; I keep the pump settings on a card beside the line. Retirement comes up at dinner, but we have not proved that stopping work would cover our rent and other costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the candle crew a clever order sheet still will not centre a wick in wet wax. We would keep checking the first jar after a fill change, which is what the customer actually burns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage and Marta's cleaning pay cover the rent, and three months saved gives us a little room for a repair. A modest office shortcut would leave my machine shift alone. I am still learning the pump, so that familiar work is welcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the wick guide and showing the first cooling jar to the lead. If an extra paid packing shift is offered before the winter rush, I would put some of that new wage into a repair reserve after food and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work. The machine needs attention, and I can ask a person when the wax does something odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a wick is off centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wick leans toward the glass while the wax is still soft, then the candle burns badly. Last Friday the lead had me stop a tray before another row was filled. A candle wick against the glass is a fault no tidy order sheet can fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the extra shift is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there is no new saving from it. I will keep the three months already put by for a gap in pay, rather than move the same money between accounts and pretend it grew.

I would keep the **first cooling jar** beside the lead before a full tray runs.
think: Our **ordinary wages** and three-month reserve cover current rent and food.
The mild software change leaves my **machine shift** familiar while I learn it.
do: **Keep** running candle filler and checking first wick with the lead.
**Save** part of newly paid extra shift wages after household bills.
feel: **Calm** about the current job and household money.
S0.quote: A candle wick against the glass is a fault no tidy order sheet can fix.
fieldNote: He is **still learning** the filler, making the lead's first-jar check a meaningful safety and quality step.
The **reserve addition** needs an offered paid shift; existing three-month savings remain for real income gaps.

steps.text: Keep filling candle jars and checking first wicks with lead
Save part of offered extra paid packing shifts after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may book wax and write delivery lists before a robot can handle a hot pump. I would ask the owner to show the paid roster before putting a camera on our filling line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One operator might be asked to watch two fillers if a new system counts jars and finds crooked wicks. I am the newer person on this machine, so my hours could be the ones to shrink. Marta's classroom wage and three months saved would not replace a whole factory week for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed roster with my last four pay slips, then keep checking the first jar by hand. If the plant requires a new pump-guard lesson and offers a paid trainer on a stopped machine, I would take it. If my base hours are actually cut, I would apply only to posted nearby filling or packing work with safe duties, base pay and bus travel that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my paid hours. I can learn a guard from a skilled person, but I will not buy a screen course to prove I deserve a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guard lesson have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would stop the pump, isolate the heater and let me clear a test spill after the wax cools. A video does not teach where hot wax can reach your wrist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What base wage would you accept nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted rate after bus fare with rent, food and the electricity bill. A promise of weekend overtime would not cover a lower regular wage.

say: I would ask for a **posted paid roster** before cameras change the candle line.
A **pump guard** should be taught on a stopped machine by a real trainer.
think: My **newer filler shift** could shrink under a two-machine roster.
Marta's wage and **three months saved** cannot replace my regular pay indefinitely.
do: **Compare** proposed candle shifts with four actual pay slips.
**Take** required pump-guard training only if a paid stopped-machine trainer place is offered.
**Apply** after actual cuts only to posted safe nearby work whose base wage survives bus and household costs.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic lost hours, while willing to learn the physical guard.
S1.quote: A video does not teach where hot wax can reach your wrist.
fieldNote: His **resistance to AI** does not block required paid practical teaching on a stopped hot-wax pump.
The **job search** depends on actual hour cuts and posted safe work whose regular wage remains usable after bus fare.

steps.text: Compare proposed candle roster with four paid slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta that AGI could plan candle orders by 2028, while capable robots that fill and inspect the physical jars follow around 2031. I would ask the owner which paid shifts remain before anyone orders new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when those robots can fill the line. I expect the newer operators to lose their shifts first, including me. Marta's cleaning pay and our three months saved will not meet rent and food for years, and I would lie awake hearing the pump stop in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put off replacing the sitting-room sofa and keep the money for rent. If the factory offers a recognised candle-quality course with funded fees, paid release and supervised practice at a guarded stopped filler, I would take it. After qualifying, if my filling hours end, I would apply only for posted safe local quality work with base pay and bus travel that cover our bills; if no course place opens, I would apply for posted safe nearby packing jobs under the same terms while keeping any paid filler shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of my wage. Three months of savings will let us breathe, but not live on a promise of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a candle-quality test include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the wick position, let a test jar cool and stop the filler before touching a jam. The trainer must watch me reject a bad tray on a guarded machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could retirement replace the filling wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual pension figures and Marta's wage cover rent, food and the bills. We have not seen that calculation yet, so I would keep searching for paid work if the candle line closes.

say: I would distinguish **2028 order planning** from capable jar-filling robots around 2031.
I would ask the owner for **remaining paid shifts** before equipment changes.
think: At **63**, I expect my newer filling shift to disappear.
Three months saved and one **cleaning wage** cannot cover our living costs for long.
do: **Postpone** the sitting-room sofa and keep cash for rent.
**Take** recognised quality training only if funded paid guarded supervised place is offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local quality if qualified, or packing without a course, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless household worry.
S2.quote: Three months of savings will let us breathe, but not live on a promise of work.
fieldNote: His **hands-on filling risk** comes around 2031, three years after AGI changes order planning.
The **qualified quality route** and independent packing fallback require real safe local postings and adequate pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may handle wax orders by 2031, with capable robots doing the physical filling around 2034. Five years gives us a chance to learn a real testing job while the old line still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots reach the jars. I might still need paid work then; our three-month reserve is not a pension. There are some nearby factories, but I would have to see an actual posted wage before treating another job as a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take any offered paid extra day and put new money toward a larger reserve after bills. I would enroll in a recognised product-testing course only if the employer funds tuition, pays release hours and offers guarded practice with a trainer. After passing, if filling hours fall, I would apply for posted safe local testing only if its base rate after bus fare covers our bills; without a workable course, I would search posted packing jobs on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later shifts, but five years gives me time to learn beside someone competent. A lesson in a room is not proof I can stop a hot filler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical assessment ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a cooled jar, catch a leaning wick and isolate the hot pump before a trainer signs the result. I cannot learn where wax spills by clicking through photographs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a distant testing post work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would calculate the bus fare and shift end against the posted base wage before applying. A far-away job that costs the pay rise in travel is no improvement.

say: I would ask for **paid product testing** before robots reach candle filling around 2034.
A **posted base wage** matters more than a course title.
think: At **66**, I may still need a regular factory wage.
Three months saved and **possible local jobs** do not settle retirement affordability.
do: **Save** new wages from offered extra paid days after household bills.
**Enroll** in recognised testing only with funded tuition, paid release and guarded trainer practice.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts to posted safe testing, or packing without a course, at viable base pay.

S3.quote: A far-away job that costs the pay rise in travel is no improvement.
fieldNote: He needs **actual guarded practice** with a trainer before treating product testing as a usable second skill.
The **testing application** follows qualification and cuts; packing remains a separate fallback with posted pay after bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan candle orders in 2036, while capable robots could fill the jars around 2039. A decade is time to put paid apprenticeships and real job terms on paper, if the factory wants workers to plan honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when capable robots reach the line, if I am still working. Marta and I might retire before that, but there is no reason to promise it until we see whether income covers rent, food and heating. Our ordinary wages and three-month reserve make the present manageable, not the future guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid filling shifts and request written retirement figures alongside our current costs this year. If the plant offers a recognised paid candle-check course with a trainer and guarded practice while my wage continues, I would take it. If I am still working after 2036 and filling hours fall, I would apply only for posted safe nearby packing or testing roles with a base wage after travel that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, comfortable enough with the wages we have now. I will let our retirement income and rent tell me when we can stop, not the candles on a birthday cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask about the retirement figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the pension administrator for a written estimate and sit with Marta over our rent and food totals. Our grown daughter could help read a difficult page, but her wages are her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A paid guarded place while I keep the factory wage is worth doing; a self-funded class without a posted job is not. I would rather save that tuition for the bills.

say: I would ask for **paid apprenticeships** before 2039 jar-filling robots arrive.
A **decade** does not guarantee that retirement income covers rent.
think: At **71**, I might still need factory wages if retirement costs do not balance.
Our **three-month reserve** helps now but cannot guarantee a distant exit.
do: **Keep** paid candle shifts while requesting written retirement figures.

**Apply** after 2036 cuts if still working to posted safe local work at bill-covering pay after travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant work, with retirement dependent on actual written figures.
S4.quote: I will let our retirement income and rent tell me when we can stop, not the candles on a birthday cake.
fieldNote: His **retirement request** seeks an estimate against real costs; it does not imply an early or affordable exit.
A **course and later job** each need real paid safe terms, and the present filling wage continues until a suitable offer.

steps.text: Keep working paid candle-filling shifts while available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take my filling shift before Marta and I know whether we can retire. Paid guarded instruction, written shift dates and posted safe local work whose wage covers our bills would help. I would want a real retirement estimate beside our rent figure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the first candle after the filler is reset. A jar can look full and still burn badly if the wick leans into the glass. Somebody has to be paid to stop that tray.

headlineQuote: A jar can look full and still burn badly if the wick leans into the glass.
portrait: **Omar**, 58, is a junior candle-filling operator with secondary education who is still learning hot-wax machine settings.
He and his **classroom-cleaner wife** Marta have grown children, typical operator pay and three months of expenses saved.
He has **never used AI**, prefers familiar checks and accepts new work only after paid hands-on teaching and posted wages.
Fast **2031 robots** alarm him about lost factory pay; later retirement remains conditional on actual income after living costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable candle-filling robots around 2031 before he knows whether retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written shift dates**, funded guarded training, posted safe local work and a retirement estimate against real bills.
